title: Ambrose (c. 339–397)
hook: the crowd shouts Ambrose for bishop before he's even baptized

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin's cloak: one half for the man at the gate, one half for Martin. Your line was half a cloak.

The church in Milan is about to turn into a riot. The bishop has died, and the city has to choose a new one. Two parties are packed inside, shouting: those who follow the teaching of Arius, and those who hold to the creed of Nicaea, the same quarrel we met in the Arian question. So the governor of the province comes down himself to keep the peace, a trained lawyer and a public official. His name is Ambrose. He stands up and starts talking the room down. And then, over his voice, somebody shouts his name.
screen: `A CHURCH ABOUT TO RIOT.` → `THE GOVERNOR COMES TO KEEP THE PEACE.` → `SOMEBODY SHOUTS HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: The account comes from Paulinus, who served as Ambrose's secretary and wrote his life after his death. Paulinus says that while Ambrose was speaking, a child's voice cried out: Ambrose, bishop! And the whole crowd took it up. Both parties, who agreed on nothing, suddenly agreed on him. Here's the catch. Ambrose was not a priest. He wasn't even baptized. He was a catechumen, still preparing for baptism, a public official with a career. So he tried to get out of it, and some of the attempts are almost comic. He tried acting harsh in court, to seem unfit. He slipped out of the city by night, heading for another town, and, Paulinus says, wandered all night and found himself at the gate of Milan in the morning. He hid at a friend's country estate, and the friend gave him up. In the end he said yes. He was baptized, and days later made bishop. Later Ambrose wrote about it himself, in a book on the duties of the clergy. He says he was carried off from the judge's bench and the robes of office into the priesthood, and so he began to teach before he had learned. He had to learn and teach at the same time. A bishop, putting that in writing. He wasn't ready, he said so, and he took the job anyway, learning as he went.
screen: `A CHILD'S VOICE: AMBROSE, BISHOP!` · `HE TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.` · `BAPTIZED, THEN MADE BISHOP.` · `TEACHING BEFORE LEARNING.` · then, large: `CHOSEN BEFORE READY.`

segments.voice: Name one thing in front of you that you keep stepping around because you don't feel qualified: a role at work, looking after a parent, leading something small. Notice the reasons you've been giving for saying no, then picture the first small step you could take while you learn. If you pray, ask for help with it.
Ambrose. The governor in Milan whom a crowd made bishop before he was baptized, and who said he had to learn and teach at the same time. Today's word.
Your line: chosen before ready. Being ready can come along the way, as you learn. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Ambrose as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and Milan's own liturgical tradition, the Ambrosian rite, still bears his name.

notes: Paulinus, Life of Ambrose 6–9 paraphrased: dispute between Arians and Catholics over the succession; Ambrose as governor (consularis) intervening; a child's voice 'Ambrosium episcopum'; the crowd taking it up; his attempts to avoid office (severity on the tribunal, a night flight that ended at Milan's gate, hiding on the estate of Leontius, who gave him up); baptism, then ordination as bishop within days (Paulinus: on the eighth day). Confirm details, and confirm Paulinus as Ambrose's secretary (notarius).

On the Duties of the Clergy 1.1.4 paraphrased (carried off from the tribunal and insignia of office to the priesthood; began to teach before learning; must learn and teach at once). Not quoted because the exact wording of the public-domain Schaff (NPNF) translation was not verified.

Editor pass: cut 'he started reading, hard', which went beyond the cited passage, and replaced it with 'learning as he went' (from 'learn and teach at once'); changed 'a good speaker, calm in a crowd' (unsourced) to 'a trained lawyer and a public official'.
Second editor pass: replaced the myth item 'Ambrose wasn't yet baptized' with one on the child's cry, since day 730's myth already tested 'not yet baptized' (Martin as catechumen).
The previous bishop (Auxentius, an Arian) is not named. howItsDone: Doctor of the Church and Ambrosian rite; confirm wording.

Audit pass: the original game's stress on episcopum was wrong (eh-pees-KO-poom); the penult is short, so Latin stresses the antepenult: eh-PEES-ko-poom. Facts in the voice checked against Paulinus 6–9 and De officiis 1.1.4; no other change.
